Monday. Madhav lay awake till two, running through the bridge inspection in his head. At the site he checked the bolts on the east rail twice, and found one sheared. His supervisor, Ritu, raised her eyebrows. "Good catch."
Thursday. The worry came again, this time about a report he'd already finished. He wrote it down: "Alarm: report. Evidence: checked twice, Ritu approved." He read it back, let it go, and went for a swim.
The next Monday. Before the new site visit he blocked forty minutes after lunch as "recovery", no calls. He noticed the tight face of the new trainee and quietly walked her through the checklist. "You could tell I was nervous?" she asked. "I know that look," Madhav said.

qa.q: What did Madhav find on the east rail?
qa.a: He found one bolt sheared.

qa.q: What was Madhav thinking when he wrote "Alarm: report" on Thursday?
qa.a: He was treating the worry as a signal to check, then deciding from the evidence that the report was already fine.

qa.q: What choice did Madhav make before the new site visit?
qa.a: He blocked forty minutes after lunch for recovery, building rest into his work.

qa.q: How might the trainee feel when Madhav walks her through the checklist?
qa.a: She feels noticed and relieved, since he picked up on her nerves without her saying so.

grounding: Over two weeks, a young engineer whose worry catches a real fault learns to treat the alarm as information and builds rest into work.

passage: Aadhya, I've seen you checking the drawings at midnight. Let me tell you about a young architect I knew, thirty years ago, the worrier of the office. He saw every leaking roof before it leaked. He once stopped a staircase being built because the rise looked wrong by a few millimetres, and he was right. Clients loved him. But he believed every worry meant disaster, and by thirty he was so worn out he couldn't draw a straight line. That young man was me, Ramesh. My senior taught me to ask, "Is this alarm telling me to check, or telling me I've failed?" If it's check, I check. If it's failed, I rest and look again in the morning. Now go home, Aadhya. The drawings will still be here.

qa.q: What did the young architect once stop being built?
qa.a: A staircase, because the rise looked wrong by a few millimetres.

qa.q: What did young Ramesh believe every worry meant?
qa.a: He believed every worry meant disaster.

qa.q: What question did Ramesh learn to ask, and how does it help?
qa.a: "Is this alarm telling me to check, or telling me I've failed?" It lets him check when needed and rest instead of spiralling.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel on realising the worrier in the story was Ramesh?
qa.a: Aadhya may feel less alone and see the worrying as a strength to manage, not a flaw.

grounding: A senior architect tells a junior how his worrying caught real risks, and how he learned to read the alarm as information and to rest.

Wednesday
My stomach dropped this morning at the site when I saw the scaffold clamp on the east side. Everyone else walked past. Pooja said, 'You worry about everything, yaar.' True. But I asked the foreman to check anyway, and two bolts were loose. He tightened them, and nobody climbed till it was done. The site manager thanked me in front of everyone. I felt proud, and also shaky for an hour after. Then at night the same alarm started ringing about the budget meeting, the rain forecast, my mother's knee. I tried what I'd read: write each one down, then ask, is this information or a verdict? The clamp was information. Most of tonight is noise. I've blocked Saturday morning for a long walk and nothing else.
Swati

passage: At the seed cooperative in the kasba of Wardha, Dhruv was known as the one who fretted. When the new lot of cotton seed arrived before sowing season, he couldn't stop thinking about the sacks at the bottom of the truck, the ones that had sat in the rain at the railway yard. 'They're sealed,' Saurabh said. 'You worry too much.' Dhruv opened three anyway. Two smelled of damp; the seed had begun to spoil. They pulled forty sacks before a single farmer bought one. That night Saurabh brought him tea. 'All right. Your worrying saved us.' Dhruv laughed, but his shoulders stayed tight; all week he had been thinking of the farmers who might have lost a season. His wife had been telling him to rest. On Sunday, for once, he left his phone at home and sat by the river till noon.

qa.q: How many sacks did they pull?
qa.a: Forty sacks.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling about the sacks before he opened them?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and couldn't stop thinking about the ones that had sat in the rain.

qa.q: What did Dhruv do on Sunday, and why does it matter?
qa.a: He left his phone at home and sat by the river; building in rest keeps his useful alarm from wearing him out.

qa.q: How does Saurabh's view of Dhruv's worrying change?
qa.a: Saurabh first thought he worried too much, then admitted the worrying had saved them.

grounding: Shows a young professional whose worry catches a real risk early and whose concern for others runs deep, learning to build rest into work.

passage:
Two days before the riverside food festival in Melbourne, Jin couldn't stop checking the forecast. Wind, then maybe rain. Her chest tightened, and she walked the site again with a clipboard.
"You'll wear the grass out," Jamal teased.
But on that walk she noticed the stalls near the water shared one power line and had no backup. She wrote it down, called the supplier, and booked a spare generator.
Saturday afternoon the storm hit early. Half the lights failed, then flickered back on the generator. Jamal found her by the ticket tent. "Okay. Your worrying saved us."
Jin laughed, but she was shaking with tiredness. On Monday she did something new: she blocked out Tuesday afternoon in the shared calendar as rest, and wrote on a sticky note, "Alarm = information. Check it, then decide."

qa.q: What did Jin notice on her walk around the site?
qa.a: The stalls near the water shared one power line and had no backup.

qa.q: What was Jin feeling in the days before the festival?
qa.a: She felt anxious; her chest tightened and she kept checking the forecast and walking the site again.

qa.q: What did Jin learn to do with her worry after the festival?
qa.a: She treated it as information to check before deciding, and she planned rest by blocking out Tuesday afternoon.

qa.q: How does Jamal see Jin's worrying by the end?
qa.a: At first he teased her, but after the storm he said her worrying saved them, so he now sees it as useful.

grounding: Shows a worried professional whose alarm catches a real risk early and who learns to treat it as information and to plan rest.
